entry: Speech by [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] delivered on August 28, 1963, at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Delivered to over 250,000 civil rights supporters from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in [[Washington, D.C.]], it called for civil and economic rights and an end to legalized racism in the United States. King departed from his prepared text to improvise the peroration on the theme "I have a dream." Ranked the top American speech of the 20th century in a 1999 poll of public-address scholars, it is among the most iconic speeches in American history.

Chinese-American architect. Ieoh Ming Pei was born in [[Guangzhou]] and moved to the United States in 1935 to study architecture at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], transferring to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. After MIT he attended Harvard's Graduate School of Design. From 1948 he was an in-house architect for a New York developer, and in 1955 he founded I. M. Pei & Associates, later reorganized as Pei Cobb Freed & Partners. His first major recognition came with the Mesa Laboratory in Colorado, and he was chief architect of the [[John F. Kennedy]] Library in Massachusetts. Other works include Dallas City Hall, the East Building of the National Gallery of Art, and a glass pyramid for the [[Louvre]] in Paris, which sparked controversy in the early 1980s. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1983.

English former cricketer and crossbench peer. An all-rounder, Botham represented England in Test and One-Day International cricket and scored 14 Test centuries, with a highest score of 208. He played most of his first-class cricket for Somerset and was part of England squads that finished as runners-up at the 1979 and 1992 [[Cricket World Cup|Cricket World Cups]]. Botham has raised money for childhood leukaemia research, including over 13 million pounds for Bloodwise, and in 2020 it was announced he would join the [[House of Lords]] as a crossbench peer. He has chaired Durham County Cricket Club since 2017.

British writer best known for the [[James Bond]] series of spy novels. Fleming worked as a journalist and served in Britain's Naval Intelligence Division during the Second World War, drawing on that work for his fiction. He wrote his first Bond novel, *Casino Royale*, in 1952; 11 more Bond novels and two short-story collections followed between 1953 and 1966. The novels center on James Bond, an officer of the Secret Intelligence Service, commonly known as [[MI6]]. The Bond stories have sold over 100 million copies worldwide. Fleming also wrote the children's story *Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang*.

English actor known for Shakespearean stage roles and fantasy films. Widely considered one of Britain's greatest actors, he won a Tony Award for playing Antonio Salieri in *Amadeus* and has received several Laurence Olivier Awards. He was nominated for two [[Academy Awards]] and played [[Gandalf]] in *The Lord of the Rings* films and [[Magneto (Marvel Comics)|Magneto]] in the *X-Men* films. Knighted by Queen [[Elizabeth II]] in 1991, he came out as gay in 1988 and co-founded Stonewall, an LGBT rights lobby group in the United Kingdom named after the [[Stonewall riots]].

City, capital of Oyo State, southwestern Nigeria. Its metropolitan area had an estimated 4,144,130 residents in 2025, and at 3,080 sq km it is the country's largest city by land area. Ibadan came into existence in 1829 as a war camp, and in the 19th century it was the capital of the Ibadan Republic, one of the most powerful states in Yorubaland. Under British colonial rule it became the administrative centre of the old Western Region. Today it is a major commercial and research centre and a transit point between the coast and the interior. The University of Ibadan, established in 1948, was Nigeria's first autonomous university. Ibadan joined the [[UNESCO]] Global Network of Learning Cities in 2016, and its principal inhabitants are the [[Yoruba people]].

Peninsula in southwestern [[Europe]]. Mostly separated from the rest of the continent by the [[Pyrenees]], it includes [[Spain]] and [[Portugal]], as well as [[Andorra]], [[Gibraltar]] and a small part of France. With an area of approximately 583,254 sq km, it is the second-largest European peninsula after the Scandinavian Peninsula. The name is associated with the Ebro River, which the Greeks called Ibēros, though its origin remains uncertain. The interior is dominated by the central Meseta plateau, and rivers including the Douro, Tagus, Guadiana and Ebro flow from the highlands to the Atlantic or Mediterranean. Its climate ranges from Mediterranean in the east to oceanic in the northwest.

Group of long-legged wading birds with downcurved bills, in the family Threskiornithidae. Ibises inhabit wetlands, forests and plains, Many breed in large colonies, and most nest in trees, often with spoonbills or [[Heron|herons]]. They are monogamous and highly territorial while nesting and feeding, and usually feed in groups, probing mud for [[Crustacean|crustaceans]]. There are 29 extant species, plus six species of spoonbills in the same family. Two extinct genera were flightless: the Apteribis of the [[Hawaiian Islands]] and the Xenicibis of [[Jamaica]]. The sacred ibis, *Threskiornis aethiopicus*, was venerated in [[Ancient Egypt]] as a symbol of wisdom linked to the god [[Thoth]].

Spanish island in the Mediterranean Sea, the third largest of the [[Balearic Islands]]. It lies off the eastern coast of the [[Iberian Peninsula]], 150 km from [[Valencia]]. It is known for its nightlife and [[Electronic dance music|electronic dance music]] club scene, which draws large numbers of tourists in summer. Phoenician settlers founded a port there in 654 BC, and the island later came under [[Carthage]]. Ibiza and the nearby island of Formentera are a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]; together they are called the Pine Islands. Its highest point, Sa Talaiassa, is 475 metres above sea level.

Andalusian Sufi scholar, mystic, poet and philosopher. He is regarded as the first to explicitly delineate the doctrine of *waḥdat al-wujūd* (the transcendent unity of being), which holds that all things are manifestations of a single reality. His family moved to [[Seville]] when he was a child, and he later lived in [[Mecca]], Anatolia and Baghdad before settling in [[Damascus]] in 1223. After his death he was called *al-Shaykh al-Akbar* ("The Greatest Shaykh"), which gave its name to the Akbari school of [[Sufism]]. Critics, including [[Ibn Taymiyya]], accused him of pantheism. His major works include *Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam* (*The Bezels of Wisdom*).

Maghrebi traveller, explorer and scholar from Tangier, Morocco, born into a family of Islamic legal scholars. Between 1325 and 1354 he visited much of Africa, Asia and the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. He set out in 1325 on a pilgrimage (*hajj*) to [[Mecca]] and did not return to Morocco for 24 years. He served as a qadi (judge) in the [[Delhi Sultanate]] for eight years and was briefly chief judge in the [[Maldives]]. He travelled around 117,000 km in total, more than [[Zheng He]] (about 50,000 km) or [[Marco Polo]] (24,000 km). Near the end of his life he dictated an account of his journeys, known as *The Rihla*.

Founder and first king of [[Saudi Arabia]], reigning from 1932 to 1953. Abdulaziz bin Abdul Rahman Al Saud, known in the West as Ibn Saud, reconquered [[Riyadh]] in 1902 after his family had been exiled from it. Over three decades he extended his rule across most of central and northern Arabia, conquering the [[Hejaz]] in 1925; by 1932 he had extended his dominions into what became the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. His campaigns ended chronic intertribal warfare but involved brutal suppressions, including of the 1929–1930 Ikhwan revolt against his authority. He ordered the demolition of several shrines, in line with Wahhabi beliefs. He presided over the discovery of [[Petroleum|petroleum]] in 1938, and large-scale oil production began after World War II.

Sunni Muslim jurist and theologian of the Hanbali school. Born in Harran, he was taught Islamic jurisprudence by his grandfather and father in [[Damascus]]. He argued that reason and revelation do not contradict each other, and he rejected philosophy as a prerequisite for religious truth. Clerics and state authorities accused him of [[Anthropomorphism|anthropomorphism]], and his condemnation of Sufi practices associated with saint veneration led to several imprisonments. His doctrines influenced [[Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab]], founder of the Wahhabism reform movement, and later Islamist groups, including the [[Muslim Brotherhood]], [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]] and [[Islamic State]], cited his teachings. Portrayals of him as anti-Sufi are widely considered inaccurate; he praised many Sufi masters and was affiliated with the Qadiriyya order.

Arab physicist, mathematician and astronomer, known in the West as Alhazen. Born in [[Basra]], he spent most of his productive years in [[Cairo]] under the [[Fatimid Caliphate]], earning his living by writing treatises and tutoring. His *Kitāb al-Manāẓir* (*Book of Optics*), written between 1011 and 1021, paved the way for modern physical optics, and he is referred to as the "father of modern optics." He correctly argued that vision is intromissive, with light entering the eye, and that vision occurs in the brain. He gave the first complete statement of the law of reflection. His work was frequently cited during the Scientific Revolution by [[Galileo Galilei]], [[René Descartes]], [[Johannes Kepler]] and [[Christiaan Huygens]].

Burkinabé military officer and interim president of [[Burkina Faso]] since 2022. He led a coup in September 2022 that ousted Paul-Henri Sandaogo Damiba, becoming at 34 the world's youngest head of state at the time. He has distanced the country from [[France]], expelled French troops and aligned it with [[Russia]], [[Turkey]] and [[China]], and helped found the Alliance of Sahel States with [[Mali]] and [[Niger]]. Supporters praise his pan-Africanist and anti-imperialist policies. Critics cite a crackdown on the press and political opposition, including the unlawful conscription of critics and journalists.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain, fever and [[Inflammation|inflammation]]. It works by decreasing the activity of the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX), which reduces prostaglandin production. Discovered in 1961 in [[Nottingham]] by Stewart Adams and John Nicholson, it was first sold in 1969 in the United Kingdom as Brufen. Long-term use has been associated with kidney failure and, rarely, [[Liver|liver]] failure. At higher doses it may increase the risk of [[Myocardial infarction|heart attack]], and it can worsen [[Asthma|asthma]]. It is not recommended in later [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. It is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

Figure in [[Greek mythology]], son of the craftsman Daedalus. Imprisoned with his father on [[Crete]] by King Minos, the two escaped using wings of feathers and beeswax. Daedalus warned Icarus not to fly too low or too close to the [[Sun|sun]], but Icarus flew too high, the wax melted, and he fell into the sea and drowned. The sea near the island of Icaria is called the Icarian Sea. The fullest account is in [[Ovid]]'s *Metamorphoses*, and the story gave rise to the idiom "fly too close to the Sun."

Solid state of water, forming at or below 0 °C (32 °F). Ice is a naturally occurring crystalline solid, considered a [[Mineral|mineral]]. Virtually all ice on Earth has a hexagonal crystal structure, ice Ih, in which [[Hydrogen bond|hydrogen bonds]] control many of its physical properties. Ice is about 8.3% less dense than liquid water, so it floats, and it expands about 9% when freezing. As snow and hail it is a common form of [[Precipitation|precipitation]], and it forms [[Glacier|glaciers]] and [[Ice sheet|ice sheets]] on land. Ice volume has been decreasing because of [[Climate change]], and the loss of grounded ice is the primary contributor to sea level rise. Humans have used ice to store food for thousands of years, before refrigeration; some ice-storage structures are over 2,000 years old.

American rapper, songwriter and actor, born O'Shea Jackson in [[Los Angeles]]. As lead rapper of [[N.W.A]], he wrote most of the lyrics for *Straight Outta Compton*, helping shape West Coast hip-hop. He left the group in late 1989 after a monetary dispute over its management. His solo albums include *AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted* (1990). He made his acting debut in *Boyz n the Hood* (1991) and co-wrote the comedy *Friday* (1995), which spawned a franchise. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] as a member of N.W.A in 2016.

American rapper and actor, born Tracy Lauren Marrow in [[Newark, New Jersey]]. Active in [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] and [[Heavy metal music|heavy metal]], he released *Power* (1988), his only platinum album. He co-founded the heavy metal band Body Count in 1990. Controversy over the song "Cop Killer" led him to ask to be released from his Warner Bros. Records contract. Since 2000 he has played detective Odafin Tutuola in *Law & Order: Special Victims Unit*, making him, according to Deadline, the longest-running male series actor in American TV history.

Period of long-term cooling of Earth's surface and atmosphere, marked by prolonged expansion of continental [[Glacier|glaciers]] and polar ice caps. Ice ages contain colder glacial periods alternating with warmer interglacials. Earth is in the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, which began 34 million years ago, and the Quaternary glaciation began 2.58 million years ago. The most recent glacial period, the [[Last Glacial Period]], was followed by the warm [[Holocene]], which began 11,700 years ago. The [[Last Glacial Maximum]] peaked between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Scientific understanding developed slowly: in 1795 [[James Hutton]] explained erratic boulders in the Alps by the action of glaciers, and in 1824 Jens Esmark proposed that changes in climate, linked to changes in Earth's orbit, caused a sequence of ice ages.

Frozen dessert typically made from [[Milk|milk]] or [[Cream|cream]], sweetened and flavored with a spice such as [[Vanilla|vanilla]] or with fruit. The mixture is cooled below the freezing point of water and stirred to incorporate air and prevent large ice crystals from forming. It is served in dishes or cones, or in desserts such as sundaes, milkshakes and Baked Alaska. *Gelato*, the Italian word for ice cream, is often used in English. The history likely began in ancient Persia around 550 BC, when Persian techniques for storing ice led to early frozen desserts. In many countries the name is legally defined: in the United States and the United Kingdom, the term applies only to products meeting a specification based largely on butterfat from cream.

Team sport played on ice skates by two teams of six players on a rink. Teams score by shooting a vulcanized rubber puck into the opponent's net with their sticks, and each goal is worth one point. The team with more goals after three 20-minute periods wins, and ties are broken in overtime or a shootout. The modern sport was developed in Canada, most notably in [[Montreal]], where the first indoor game was played on March 3, 1875. It draws influence from [[Field hockey]] and from shinty. The Stanley Cup, first awarded in 1893, became the championship trophy of the [[National Hockey League|NHL]]. Ice hockey was first played at the Olympics at the 1920 Summer Games and is now a mainstay of the Winter Games. In 1994 it was officially recognized as Canada's national winter sport.

Mass of glacial ice covering more than 50,000 sq km of land, also called a continental glacier. Ice sheets are the largest glacial bodies on Earth. The two that exist today are the [[Antarctic ice sheet]], covering 14 million sq km, and the [[Greenland ice sheet]], covering 1.7 million sq km. Ice sheets flow outward from central domes, moving faster in ice streams where meltwater lubricates the base. At the maximum of the [[Last Glacial Period]], the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets merged with the Greenland ice sheet to cover much of North America. The ongoing retreat of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets plays a major role in [[Climate change]] and sea level rise.

Large platform of glacial ice floating on the ocean, fed by one or more tributary glaciers. Ice shelves form along coastlines where the ice is too thin to displace the denser seawater, and they are found in [[Antarctica]] and the [[Arctic]], including along Greenland, northern Canada and the Russian Arctic. The largest are the Ross Ice Shelf and the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in Antarctica, and the aggregate area of Antarctic ice shelves exceeds 1,550,000 sq km. Shelves range from about 100 to 1,000 m thick and act as brakes on the glaciers that feed them; without them, glaciers may speed up. Glaciologists have observed decreases in ice shelf extent through melt, calving and the complete disintegration of some shelves, such as the Thwaites and Larsen ice shelves.
